item.aggregated_output: {"id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","track":"held_out","category":"convergent_evolution","prompt":"NAD(P)-binding enzymes occur in multiple SCOP folds and superfamilies. What does this imply about convergent versus divergent evolution, and why is cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone insufficient evidence of homology?"}

item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"NAD(P) binding is a recurring biochemical solution, not by itself a single homology signal. In SCOPe terms, enzymes that bind NAD or NADP can be found in different folds and superfamilies, for example the alpha/beta Rossmann-like NAD(P)-binding fold class/fold region such as c.2, but also other unrelated folds that use different overall architectures to bind the same dinucleotide cofactor. Members of the same family imply close homologs; members of the same superfamily support probable common ancestry despite low sequence identity; members of the same fold share a similar major architecture but need not be homologous; members only in the same class are still weaker evidence. Therefore, NAD(P)-dependent activity across different SCOPe folds is best interpreted as convergent evolution of cofactor use unless independent evidence places the proteins in the same homologous superfamily. Cofactor binding alone is unsafe because NAD(P) imposes common physical and chemical constraints, so unrelated proteins can evolve similar glycine-rich phosphate-binding loops, charged residues near the pyrophosphate, or active-site acid/base chemistry. Active-site similarity alone is also insufficient: catalytic residues and ligand-contact geometries can converge under the same reaction chemistry. Functional annotation, homology transfer, representative selection, and template-based modeling should therefore not be transferred merely because two proteins bind NAD(P) or have a superficially similar active site; transfer is strongest within a family, often reasonable within a well-supported superfamily with conserved mechanism, and much more limited across fold or class boundaries without external evidence such as statistically significant sequence similarity, conserved domain architecture, structural alignment beyond the binding pocket, and phylogenetic support.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
